extracted.intended_audience: constitutional and administrative law scholars, judges, appellate lawyers, and advanced law students
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluative and doctrinal standards for assessing delegation, agency power, and the separation of powers in U.S. constitutional law; explains historical cases and doctrinal tests and argues for a formalist reassertion of constitutional branches over administrative functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separation of powers (allocation of powers)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Constitution enshrined the separation of powers by 'vest[ing]' legislative power in Congress, 'vest[ing]' executive power in the President, and 'vest[ing]' judicial power in the courts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate government structures by whether legislative, executive, and judicial powers are allocated to the appropriate constitutional institutions; the text cites U.S. CONST. art. I, II, III and notes the Framers thought this allocation critical to preventing tyranny and preserving liberty. Examples: statutes and clauses that formally vest powers in each branch.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checks and balances (overlap as safeguard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Although powers are separate, they are not entirely separate; each branch has roles in the exercise of the others so that 'ambition must be made to counteract ambition.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether branches have 'constitutional means and personal motives to resist encroachments' by the others. Examples given: presidential veto (art. I, §7), Senate appointments/ratification (art. II, §2), impeachment roles (art. I, §3). The metric values overlapping powers that serve as mutual checks to prevent concentration of power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vesting Clauses as textual baseline
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the Vesting Clauses (Article I, §1; Article II, §1; Article III, §1) as the textual basis for separation-of-powers analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article cites these clauses as the constitutional language establishing branch allocation; use them to anchor doctrinal arguments about which branch should exercise particular functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intelligible principle test (J.W. Hampton)
rubrics_metrics.description: If Congress 'shall lay down by legislative act an intelligible principle to which the person or body authorized to fix such rates is directed to conform,' the delegation is not a forbidden delegation of legislative power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the J.W. Hampton standard to determine whether statutory delegations are constitutional: look for an intelligible principle that constrains the delegate. The piece cites case law examples and explains the historical reliance on this test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegation vs. execution distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish between delegating power to 'make the law' (impermissible) and conferring authority or discretion as to its execution, to be exercised 'under and in pursuance of the law' (permissible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate delegations by whether they leave discretion over 'what the law shall be' (invalid) versus discretion in applying/executing a law already made (valid). The article quotes state and federal precedent (e.g., Cincinnati, Wilmington & Zanesville R.R.; Minnesota railway case) illustrating the test.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity of statutory standards (sufficiency of terms)
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess whether statutory phrases (e.g., 'public convenience, interest, or necessity'; 'just and reasonable'; 'necessary or appropriate in the public interest') are precise enough to constitute an intelligible principle.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider context and technical meaning: some terms (like 'just and reasonable' in ratemaking) may be 'specific enough' as terms of art, while others (broad standards like public interest) may be too vague. Examples: FCC licensing standard (47 U.S.C. §307(a)), SEC anti-fraud provision (15 U.S.C. §78j(b)), Clean Air Act language (42 U.S.C. §7409(b)(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional (vs. formal) characterization of agency action
rubrics_metrics.description: Agency actions should be characterized by their function: rulemaking can be 'quasi-legislative' in character even if labeled 'executive.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate agency activity on its practical effects (does it promulgate rules with force of law, police compliance, adjudicate disputes?) rather than simply its formal label. The article notes courts often 'pretend' agency power is purely executive even when agencies exercise legislative and judicial functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collapse of powers in agencies (combined powers concern)
rubrics_metrics.description: Modern administrative agencies 'exercise legislative power, by promulgating regulations with the force of law; executive power, by policing compliance; and judicial power, by adjudicating enforcement actions and imposing sanctions.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Measure the degree to which agencies concentrate multiple constitutional functions in the same institution and the implications of that concentration for separation-of-powers norms. Cited authorities: City of Arlington dissent, Rosenbloom, Lawson, Strauss, Sunstein.

rubrics_metrics.name: Agency adjudication before agency adjudicators (fairness/bias metric)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate whether agencies enforce their rules 'in front of their own ALJs' (administrative law judges) and whether that practice raises structural bias or adjudicatory fairness concerns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: EPA and FCC authorization for administrative adjudications; SEC's practice of bringing enforcement actions before its own judges with high win rates (SEC wins ~90% before its judges vs ~69% in federal courts); recent circuit litigation (Hill v. SEC; Tilton v. SEC) challenge this practice. Use win-rates and circuit decisions as indicators of potential unfairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nondelegation doctrine enforcement practicalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that the nondelegation doctrine has been enforced rarely (only twice—Panama Refining and Schechter—in 1935) and that courts find the doctrine difficult to administer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating challenges to delegations, account for doctrinal and practical hurdles (as Justice Scalia noted): statutes cannot be entirely precise, policy judgments often must be left to officers, and courts are reluctant to second-guess Congress. This reduces the likelihood of successful nondelegation attacks under current precedent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formalist reassertion via constitutional administration
rubrics_metrics.description: The article proposes accepting, to some degree, unconstitutional delegation (recognizing its practical existence) while reasserting constitutional control by mapping particular administrative functions back to the appropriate constitutional branches.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As a normative rubric, measure administrative arrangements by whether doctrinal tools can be used to restore a formal separation of functions (for example, reassigning legislative, executive, or judicial control over specific administrative acts), and consider doctrines like the legislative veto in that light. The argument is pragmatic: accept historical delegation but use formalist tools to preserve separation-of-powers core.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preservation of liberty and republican government as evaluative end
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate institutional arrangements by whether they preserve liberty and the possibility of republican government, i.e., prevent concentration of power and factional capture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use historical Framers' concerns about faction and tyranny as normative benchmarks: separation of powers and checks and balances were understood as necessary not only for liberty but for republican government itself. Consider whether modern administrative arrangements undermine or support those ends.
